title: The services page a small clinic actually needs
metaTitle: The small clinic services page, in patient words
excerpt: List each clinic service in the patient's words, with the outcome, the boundary, and a way to book that visit. A grid of procedure names does not help.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk, a page already sorted for a services list that should be just as plain.
caption: A notebook, a pen, and glasses on a desk. The services should be this easy to tell apart. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a clinic name its services online?
faqs.answer: Use the words a patient says when they call. "A first visit for knee pain" is a service name, and a phrase like "musculoskeletal solutions" is a department. The heading should be something they can repeat to the front desk. If the clinical term matters, put it in the next line, not in place of their word.

faqs.question: How many services should the page include?
faqs.answer: Include the visits you want a stranger to book, each with a boundary. A small clinic often needs a handful, not a catalog. If two names always happen in the same appointment, write one visit. A long grid of procedures pushes an anxious patient back into self-diagnosis.

faqs.question: Should every service have its own booking button?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the appointment type is different. The button should book that visit, or call the desk about that visit, and the label should say which. One generic "Contact" button at the bottom of a procedure list makes every service feel like a maybe. Pass the visit name through so the desk does not have to guess.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A small clinic services page should list the work in the patient's language. For someone who is already anxious, each service needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, which is to book a visit.

A grid of procedure names does not help. It asks the patient to sort your clinical menu before they know whether they are allowed to come in. Name the jobs they already have words for.

## The reason they called, not the department

Start from the sentence a person says to a friend. "My knee has been swollen for a month." "I need a check before I go back to training." "I have a letter from my doctor and I do not know what it means." Those sentences are closer to a service than the name of a specialty. The specialty can sit in a smaller line for the patient who already knows it, and for the clinician who searches for it.

Google's guidance on title links asks for titles that describe the page and stay concise. The same rule belongs on each service heading. A heading is a title in miniature. "Comprehensive care pathways" will not survive as a title or as a thing a patient repeats at the desk. "First visit" will. If a heading only makes sense after a paragraph of context, it is not a heading yet.

Give each service a block with room to breathe. Icon grids squash the boundary, and the boundary is what an anxious reader needs. They are trying to rule themselves in or out without making a phone call they dread. A paragraph that says "this visit is for this person, and it is not for this situation" is an act of courtesy.

The page needs one purpose. Google's people-first questions ask whether a visitor can tell what the page is for, and whether they leave knowing enough to do the next thing. "Everything we treat" is not a purpose. "The visits you can book, and who each one is for" is.

## The outcome of the visit, not a promise of a cure

Write the outcome as what the patient leaves knowing or having done. A plan. A letter. A decision about whether a procedure is even appropriate. Relief from not guessing. Do not write a result you cannot promise and should not imply. A services page is not a testimonial and not a guarantee. Clinics get into trouble when the marketing sentence outruns what the clinician will say in the room.

A clean outcome sounds like this. "You leave with a written plan and a recommendation to book imaging, or not." "You leave knowing whether we are the right clinic, and a referral onward if we are not." Those sentences respect the limit of a first visit. "Get your life back" does not. Cut the poster language even if it tested well in a brand workshop. The patient on this page is not in a workshop. They are deciding whether to be vulnerable in your room.

One outcome per service. If you need three outcomes, you may have three visits, or you may be describing the whole clinic. The whole clinic belongs on the homepage as the room and the clinician. This page is the menu of visits, edited.

Use time and sequence as part of the outcome. What happens in the first few minutes, what the examination is, what the last few minutes are for. Anxious patients rehearse. A short rehearsal on the page is more useful than a list of equipment.

## The boundary, in the same block

The boundary says who should not book this visit, and what you will not do inside it. It feels like turning away revenue. It is how you keep the right people from arriving in the wrong room.

Boundaries worth writing:

- Ages you do not see, or ages you see only with a guardian present.
- Conditions or urgencies that belong in an emergency department, stated calmly, with the instruction to seek urgent care.
- What the visit will not include, such as a procedure, a prescription, or imaging on the same day.
- Whether a referral is required.
- The town or the mode: in the room, or a video visit, and which one this block is.

Write the urgent-care boundary in plain words and do not bury it. A services page must not look like a place for a crisis it cannot treat. That is a safety matter, not a brand matter. Say where to go instead, in one sentence, without a lecture.

Keep the tone flat. "This visit is not for chest pain. Call emergency services." is a complete boundary. "We are passionate about holistic journeys" is not a boundary. If a neighboring service is the right one, link it by the patient's name for it. Do not make them decode a code.

The boundary should match what the desk is trained to say. If the page says no referral and the desk asks for one, the page is a trap. Update the stricter of the two so they agree. A small clinic does not get to have a marketing policy and an operations policy.

## Book this visit, not a generic contact

End each block with the booking for that visit. The label should include the visit. "Book a first visit." "Call the desk about a follow-up." If the diary has a specific appointment type, the link should open it. A patient who has just recognized themselves should not land on a blank calendar called "Other."

If some visits cannot be booked online, say why in a clause. "The desk books this one because we need to match you with the right clinician." Then put the phone number in the block, not only in the header. Anxious patients often prefer a voice once they know what they would say. The page should give them the sentence. "Tell them you want a first visit for a swollen knee."

Do not end the block with "Learn more" unless the next page contains a fact this block cannot hold, such as preparation instructions. If you do link onward, the link text should name the fact. "How to prepare for the visit" is a reason to click. "Learn more" is a delay.

At the bottom of the page, repeat one path for people who read the boundaries and still fit. Same verb as the homepage. Book a visit. If they are unsure which block is theirs, offer the desk as the sorter, and say that the desk would rather help them choose than have them guess. That is a kinder line than a quiz.

## How many visits, and which come first

Order the page by the visits a stranger is most likely to need, not by the order your software lists appointment types. The first block should be the one the homepage already named. If the homepage is a first visit for pain, that visit should not be third under a specialist label.

A small clinic can often describe itself in four blocks. A first visit. A follow-up. A visit for an existing patient who has a new question. A visit you want people to stop booking online because it needs a conversation. That last one still belongs on the page, with the boundary, so people stop booking it wrong.

Merge names that are the same hour. If "assessment" and "initial consultation" are the same diary slot, pick the patient's word and retire the synonym. Synonyms create a fear of choosing the wrong one. Fear of choosing is a reason people do not book.

Leave intentions off the page. A treatment you hope to add next season is not a service. "Coming soon" on a clinical menu looks like the current visits might be unfinished too. Publish what the room can do this week.

## Put the room and the clinician next to the visit

Each block should remind the patient where they will be and who they will see. A single photograph of the real room can serve the page if the caption says which visits happen there. A portrait of the clinician belongs on the visits they actually take. Do not paste the same stock smile on every card. The repetition makes the menu look like a template, and it hides the fact that a specific person does this work.

If a visit is delivered by more than one clinician, say how the choice works. Patient preference, first available, or a match the desk makes. Uncertainty about "who will touch me" is a common reason people hesitate. Answer it in the block. If you cannot know until the day, say that, and say that the desk will name the person before they arrive.

Proof, if you use it, is a process fact, not a miracle. "Most first visits end with a written plan before you leave" is a process fact if it is true. A quote about being cured is a claim you should not improvise on a services page. Keep quotes for a proof page with permission and with the limit of the story intact.

When the page needs a designer and a build, not another pass in a document, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the list of appointment types from your diary. The call should separate the visits patients can name from the internal labels that only the software needs.

## Review the menu with the desk

Read every heading to the person who answers the phone. Ask which headings they would never say aloud. Rename those. Then ask which question they still have to explain that the page does not. Add that boundary. The services page is a script for the desk as much as a page for the patient. If the script and the page diverge, patients hear the divergence as disorganization, and disorganization feels unsafe.

Check the fee link. Each bookable visit should land on the fee that matches, or show it in the block. A services page with no money, and a pricing page with different names, makes the patient do reconciliation you should have done. Use one name in both places.

Open the page on a phone and tap the visit you would book if you were frightened and in a hurry. Count the steps to a confirmed type or a human. If the path dumps into a general inbox, you have a catalog, not a service. Fix the path before you polish the icons.

The people behind those visits are the next page. [How a small clinic should write an about page](/blog/how-a-small-clinic-should-write-an-about-page) covers who to name, and which origin stories help a patient book.
